                         COMMENTS OF THE DISTRICT OF COLUMBIA

          The District of Columbia (the “District”), through its Office of Attorney General and

Department of Energy and Environment, respectfully submits these comments in response to the

Complaint of the Maryland Office of People’s Counsel (“OPC”). The Complaint 1 raises concerns

shared by the District about PJM cost allocation for the transmission infrastructure needs of large

data center loads. As the Complaint indicates, existing ratepayers in jurisdictions including

Maryland and the District are being assigned substantial costs for regional baseline transmission

projects driven primarily by the projected needs of large data center development in other states.

The unique scale and characteristics of this data center load growth warrant action by the

Commission to prevent unjust and unreasonable costs that are resulting from current cost allocation

methods. Given these new circumstances, the District encourages the Commission to provide

opportunities for robust consideration of guardrails to protect ratepayers in the District and


1
 Md. Office of People’s Counsel v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al., Amended Complaint Requesting Fast Track
Processing, Docket No. EL26-63-000 (filed May 21, 2026) (“Complaint”).

                                                                                                              1
 elsewhere from shouldering data center infrastructure costs without receiving commensurate

benefits.

I. The District has a significant interest in the outcome of this proceeding.

        The District is responsible for ensuring that power for District residents and businesses

remains reliable and affordable, and for advancing the District’s energy policies. A recent study

conducted by the District’s Department of Energy and Environment (“Study”) demonstrates the

stakes of rising transmission costs for District ratepayers. 2 The District is located entirely within

the Potomac Electric Power Company (“Pepco”) transmission zone, which also includes parts of

Maryland. For residential Pepco customers, transmission rates increased by 68 percent between

2021 and 2025 – or by 44 percent even after adjusting for inflation. 3 This increase represents

roughly 9 percent of a typical residential electric bill. As of August 2025, 24 percent of Pepco’s

residential customers were already behind on paying their electric bills. 4

        The Study also notes that “load growth outside of DC and the Pepco zone is likely to

continue to drive more and more transmission project spending at an accelerating pace moving

forward, some of which will likely be allocated to the Pepco zone.” 5 This load growth disparity is

significant, with small projected increases for the District and much larger growth forecasts for

other parts of the PJM region. PJM’s 2025 load forecast projected that the regionwide load will

increase by 48 percent from 2025 to 2045, while the Pepco zone’s load will grow by only 4 percent.

The Study also notes that data center development is increasing the uncertainty of regionwide

forecasts, “creating risks of overbuilding transmission assets for load that may not materialize.” 6

 Given that load growth outside the District is becoming an outsized driver of Pepco transmission

rates, it is critical to the District for the Commission to ensure that cost allocation approaches adapt

to changing circumstances.

II. The current cost allocation methodology for transmission infrastructure driven by large
    loads is unjust and unreasonable for District ratepayers.

        The OPC Complaint estimates that, over the next decade, Maryland customers will pay

about $1.6 billion through their electric bills in additional costs for PJM Regional Transmission

Expansion Plan (“RTEP”) projects driven primarily by data center load growth occurring outside

of Maryland transmission zones. 7 The corresponding estimate for District of Columbia customers,

based on the District’s share of peak demand in the Pepco zone that it shares with Maryland, is

roughly $300 million, 8 which costs are being disproportionately triggered by projected load

growth outside the District. The Complaint notes that, over this period, “load projections for

transmission zones covering Maryland show only marginal forecasted load growth.” The same

holds true for the District, which shares the Pepco zone with Maryland. 9 The District’s Study

identifies as a “glaring trend” that PJM load forecasts are increasing primarily due to projected

development of data centers outside the District. 10 The Study emphasizes that “DC’s contribution



7
  Complaint at 2.
8
  The OPC Complaint’s $1.6 billion figure includes an estimate that customers in Maryland’s portion of the Pepco
zone will pay roughly $485 million of these additional costs (see Exhibit RN-AE-3 of the Affidavit of Ron Nelson
and Andrew Eiden). The Pepco zone is comprised of parts of Maryland and the entirety of the District of Columbia.
The Affidavit (pg. 59, footnote 110) states a conservative assumption that Maryland’s share of the Pepco total zonal
peak is 60 percent, which would (less conservatively) indicate a District of Columbia share of the Pepco total zonal
peak of the remaining 40 percent. Because the estimated Maryland Pepco customer costs of $485 million reflect a 60
percent share of the Pepco zone, the corresponding estimate of total costs (100 percent) for the Pepco zone would be
$808 million, with the remaining 40 percent share being $323 million as a less conservative estimate of the total
increased revenue requirement for District of Columbia Pepco customers over the next 10 years due to costs of
transmission projects across the last three PJM transmission expansion planning windows. Alternatively, the above-
referenced January 2026 study prepared for the District estimates that District ratepayers pay 34 percent of costs
allocated to the Pepco transmission zone (Study at 4.) Applying that 34 percent share to the Complaint’s estimates
would yield a figure of $275 million. The $300 million figure is presented as a ballpark midpoint for these two
estimates.
9

10

 to this projected load growth is negligible; PJM’s 2025 regional load forecast for the Year 2030

jumped roughly 10 percent from the previous year’s forecast, while the load for the zone containing

DC decreased by 3 percent.” 11

        Given these disparate trends, the District shares the concerns presented in the Complaint

that PJM’s current cost allocation methodology requires existing customers in Maryland, the

District, and elsewhere to “subsidize data center growth,” because “the revenue requirements for

these large transmission build outs to serve data center growth are being pooled together under the

category of ‘RTEP baseline reliability upgrades’ instead of being assigned to those causing the

costs.” 12 While some regional projects included in recent RTEP windows may indeed benefit

District ratepayers, and the District is supportive of multi-value regional transmission projects that

can bring down overall system costs, the scale and geographic concentration of data center load

presents unique risks of unjust cross-subsidization.

        Some of those risks stem from the uncertainty of data center load forecasts. This

Commission emphasized in the June 18, 2026, Order to Show Cause its “concern[] that PJM’s

existing Tariff fails to deter speculative or duplicative requests for transmission service . . . on

behalf of large loads,” which can “distort load forecasts” and “create a substantial risk of cost shifts

if the large load additions do not materialize as planned.” 13 Similarly, the Complaint notes that

“when forecasted large loads do not materialize,” the current cost allocation methodology produces

“a systematic transfer of stranded asset risk from the zones that attracted the speculative load

growth" to “ratepayers in non-causal zones.” 14 Those non-causal zones include the District.

            Under this unique set of circumstances–massive load growth driven overwhelmingly by a

single industry that is seeking transmission service at unprecedented speed and uncertain scale–

status quo approaches to cost allocation would saddle District ratepayers with significant new costs

that are not commensurate to the benefits they receive. The District echoes the comments of the

New Jersey Board of Public Utilities that “under the new paradigm in which load growth is no

longer approximately even over the zones,” and with the region instead experiencing “the new

phenomenon of very large loads from a single industry creating unprecedented forecast error and

stranded asset risk,” the “cost allocation status quo results in a level of socialization that is

incompatible with the cost-causation principle.” 15

III. Commission action is needed to change the status quo.

           A strong, widespread consensus has emerged that data centers should pay for infrastructure

costs they cause, but cost allocation approaches have not yet changed accordingly. The White

House Ratepayer Protection Pledge includes a commitment that “Companies cover all new

delivery upgrades required to service their data centers, including network upgrade costs, ensuring

those expenses are not passed on to ordinary households.” 16 Several PJM Transmission Owners,

including the Exelon Corporation (the parent company of Pepco), have signed the Ratepayer

Protection Pledge, as have 40 data center developers. But the Ratepayer Protection Pledge will not

become a reality without Commission action.

           The Commission has taken important steps forward in its June 18, 2026, Order to Show

Cause (Docket No. EL26-67-000), which expresses “concern[] that the potentially speculative

nature of requests for transmission service by Eligible Customers on behalf of large loads, the

speed and scale with which large loads are seeking to be added to the transmission system, the


15
     New Jersey Board of Public Utilities Comments at 6.
16
     The White House, https://www.whitehouse.gov/ratepayer-protection-pledge/.

                                                                                                   5
 projected need for significant Network Upgrades to provide transmission service to Eligible

Customers on behalf of large loads, and the lack of centralized information on the associated

transmission costs in PJM hamper the ability of the Commission and stakeholders (including

transmission customers and state regulators) to understand and accurately assess the relationship

between the addition of large loads to the transmission system and wholesale transmission costs.”17

In particular, the Commission “preliminarily [found] that PJM’s Tariff appears to be unjust and

unreasonable because it lacks adequate mechanisms to mitigate the risk of cost shifting among

transmission customers, which may result in unjust and unreasonable rates for transmission

service.” 18 Yet, as the OPC has noted in its Response and Answer, the Show Cause Order “is

principally directed to Supplemental Projects and other locally planned Network Upgrades” and

does not squarely address “regional baseline cost-allocation issues.” 19 The District supports a

comprehensive approach by the Commission to address the concerns identified both in the Show

Cause Order and in this proceeding.

IV. Conclusion

        The Complaint and other commenters have indicated several potential paths forward. The

District echoes in particular the suggestion of the Pennsylvania Office of Consumer Advocate that

“FERC should allow parties to develop an actionable record on regional wholesale cost allocation

methods for Network Upgrades caused by computational large loads, in EL26-67, EL26-63, or

both.” 20 The District supports a robust consideration of alternatives and is currently receiving

technical assistance from the U.S. Department of Energy National Laboratories to assess how

 different approaches to allocating large load-driven transmission costs in PJM could affect District

priorities, particularly with respect to affordability. The District encourages the Commission to use

this proceeding, the Show Cause Order proceeding, or other venues as necessary to advance

comprehensive reforms to prevent unjust and unreasonable cost shifting from new large loads to

other transmission customers.
